items.title: L7: The pre-election period
items.source: Cabinet Office, General Election Guidance; Cabinet Manual
items.body: Before a general election, Parliament is dissolved and the government continues in office but follows long-standing conventions known as the pre-election period, sometimes called purdah. The Cabinet Secretary issues guidance to departments before each election. The central idea is that the government should avoid actions that could affect the outcome of the election or commit an incoming government to a course it might not choose. Departments continue the routine business of government and must keep public services running. They avoid, unless essential, launching new major policy initiatives, making significant new appointments, entering large new contracts that could be taken as binding on an incoming government, and using public money for publicity that could favour one party. Government communications are limited to what is necessary, such as essential public safety information. Ministers remain in post and can take decisions needed for the continued running of their department, but they act with restraint. Officials must not support party-political campaigning, so ministers' special advisers leave their posts at the point of dissolution. Civil servants also handle access talks: by long-standing arrangement, the Prime Minister can authorise the Cabinet Secretary to allow opposition parties to have confidential discussions with senior officials, so they understand how a department would carry out their plans if they win. Officials keep these discussions confidential and do not share them with the governing party. Where the result is unclear, the government stays in office until a clear outcome emerges, and civil servants continue to support ministers, with guidance from the Cabinet Secretary.

questions.prompt: A department planned a large new publicity campaign about a government policy to start during the election period. What is the usual approach?

options.text: Run it as planned, because the contract was signed before the election was called
Run it in a lower-key form, but only on social media where it costs less
Pause it unless it is essential public information, since publicity must not favour a party
Run it but remove the minister's name and photograph from the materials

questions.hint: Publicity is limited during the pre-election period.

questions.prompt: What happens to special advisers when Parliament is dissolved?

options.text: They leave their posts at the point of dissolution
They continue as normal until the result is known
They move to work for the party in opposition
They switch to providing impartial advice as ordinary officials

questions.hint: Spads' appointments are tied to the minister and end at dissolution.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits the purpose of the pre-election period guidance?

options.text: To suspend all government business and decision-making until the votes are counted
To stop ministers ever taking decisions in the year of an election
To let officials choose to work for whichever party they prefer in the campaign
To avoid actions that could influence the election or tie an incoming government's hands

questions.prompt: An opposition party asks for access talks. Who authorises them?

options.text: The leader of the opposition party, who simply asks the Cabinet Secretary directly
The Prime Minister, who allows the Cabinet Secretary to arrange them
The Speaker of the House of Commons, who oversees fairness between the parties
The department's special adviser, who arranges meetings for the minister

questions.hint: Access talks need the PM's authority.

questions.prompt: During access talks an official learns details of an opposition party's plans. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Treat them as confidential and do not pass them to the governing party's ministers
Tell the minister so that the government can prepare a response to the plans
Brief the press office so that it can plan communications in good time
Share it with other departments so they can plan for the likely outcomes

questions.hint: Impartiality requires confidentiality for all parties.

questions.prompt: A routine payment run for benefit claimants falls during the pre-election period. What should happen?

options.text: It is delayed until a new government has been formed and can approve it
It goes ahead as normal, since public services must keep running
It is paused until ministers have signed off every payment personally
It is replaced by a one-off announcement explaining the payment

questions.prompt: A department wants to enter a multi-year contract worth many millions during the pre-election period. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Sign it quickly before the result changes the department's plans for the contract
Sign it but keep the terms confidential until the election result is known
Sign it after a short consultation with the main opposition party
Consider delaying it unless it is essential, because it could bind an incoming government

questions.hint: Major long-term commitments are normally avoided.

questions.prompt: The election result is unclear and no party has a majority. What is the position of civil servants?

options.text: They stop all work until a government has been formed and the cabinet appointed
They take decisions themselves in place of ministers who lack a majority
They continue to support the ministers in office until a clear outcome emerges
They report to the leader of the largest party until a Prime Minister is chosen

questions.hint: Government stays in office until a clear outcome.

items.title: L7: Machinery of government changes
items.source: Cabinet Office, Machinery of government changes guidance; Cabinet Manual
items.body: Machinery of government changes are alterations to the structure of government, for example creating a new department, merging two, or moving a policy area from one department to another. The Prime Minister decides the structure of government, using powers of the Crown. A change may be made when a new government forms or at any point in a Parliament. Many changes follow a statement or a press notice from the Prime Minister's office, and then a legal order transfers functions from one minister to another. In practice, officials start planning at once. They decide which staff, budgets, assets, contracts and records transfer, and how Parliament will be kept informed. Staff move with their work, and the Cabinet Office publishes a Statement of Practice on staff transfers so that civil servants' terms and conditions are protected where there is a transfer of undertakings. The accounting officer for the receiving department takes responsibility for the money and risks it receives. The Treasury adjusts budgets, and new Estimates may be needed, because Parliament votes money to specific departments. Select committees shift their attention, because they shadow the departments in their areas. Existing contracts, legislation and licences continue; they do not lapse because a department changes. Teams should make sure that GOV.UK pages, data sharing agreements and complaints routes are updated so the public still knows where to go. Good change management also matters for staff: officials should keep people informed and avoid uncertainty about their roles.

questions.prompt: Who decides how the departments of government are structured?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary
The Speaker
The Civil Service Commission
The Prime Minister

questions.hint: Structure is a prime ministerial power.

questions.prompt: A policy function and its team move to another department. What normally happens to the staff?

options.text: They must reapply for their jobs in the receiving department through open competition
They stay in the old department and work for the new one on loan
They move with the work, and their terms are protected under the staff transfer arrangements
They are dismissed and rehired on new contracts with the receiving department

questions.prompt: Why might new Estimates be needed after a function moves?

options.text: Because the Treasury must approve every transferred contract
Because Parliament votes money to specific departments
Because the new minister requires a new budget cycle
Because the National Audit Office requires it

questions.hint: Parliamentary control of money follows departments.

questions.prompt: A contract was signed by the old department. What is the position after the function transfers?

options.text: It continues and the receiving department takes responsibility for it
It lapses automatically and has to be tendered again by the receiving department
It stays with the old department indefinitely, even though the function has moved
It transfers only if the supplier agrees in writing to the change

questions.hint: Contracts do not lapse because of a restructure.

questions.prompt: Who becomes responsible for the transferred money and risks?

options.text: The accounting officer of the department that lost the function
The Chancellor
The accounting officer of the receiving department
The Prime Minister's principal private secretary

questions.prompt: Why do officials update GOV.UK and complaint routes after a change?

options.text: Because the Act of Parliament requires it
So the public still knows where to go
Because the Cabinet Secretary signs them off
Because it lets the new department rebrand

questions.prompt: How might Parliament's scrutiny be affected?

options.text: Select committees follow the department that now holds the function
Select committees stop scrutinising until the next year
Select committees merge automatically with the new department
The old committee keeps scrutinising the function forever

questions.prompt: What is a sensible step when planning a transfer?

options.text: Wait until the new department tells you exactly what it wants to receive
Move the team first and sort out records and contracts after the transfer
Plan only for staff, since contracts remain with the supplier whatever happens
Identify staff, budgets, assets, contracts and records to be moved

items.title: L7: Giving evidence to a select committee
items.source: Cabinet Office, Departmental Evidence and Response to Select Committees (Osmotherly Rules); House of Commons guidance
items.body: Select committees are cross-party groups of MPs who scrutinise departments and can invite witnesses to give evidence. The government's guidance on how officials should respond, often called the Osmotherly Rules, says that civil servants who appear before committees do so on behalf of their ministers and under their direction. Their role is to explain and account for government policy and the actions of the department, not to defend policy as if it were their own or to give personal views. Officials should be as helpful as they can and give accurate information. They should not mislead the committee. If a question concerns advice given to ministers, officials usually refer to the minister, because the confidentiality of advice allows ministers to receive frank advice. Officials also usually avoid commenting on matters of political controversy or the conduct of other departments. Preparation for an appearance involves a briefing pack with likely questions, an understanding of what has already been published, and checking facts. Where a witness does not know an answer, they should say so and offer to write afterwards, rather than guess. They should correct any error as soon as they notice it, by writing to the committee. The accounting officer is an exception: when the Public Accounts Committee asks, they answer personally about the propriety, regularity, value for money and feasibility of spending. Committees may request documents, and refusal should be explained and escalated, not ignored. Committee evidence is a public record and may be published.

questions.prompt: An official is asked by a committee why the minister preferred one policy to another. What is the best response?

options.text: Give their own opinion on which policy was better and explain why
Explain the factors the government has set out and refer the question of the minister's choice to the minister
Decline to attend, because choices of policy are for ministers alone
Release the private advice given to the minister so the committee can judge

questions.hint: Officials account for the department, not the choice of policy.

questions.prompt: An official does not know a figure requested. What should they do?

options.text: Give their best guess so the hearing continues smoothly
Change the subject to what they do know
Ask another witness to give a figure
Say so and offer to write to the committee afterwards

questions.prompt: Later the same day, an official realises an answer they gave was inaccurate. What should they do?

options.text: Wait for the next hearing to raise it
Leave it, since the transcript is accurate to what was said
Write to the committee promptly with the correction
Tell the press office

questions.hint: Errors should be corrected at once.

questions.prompt: When does an official answer to the committee in their own right rather than for the minister?

options.text: When the accounting officer is asked about spending propriety, regularity, value for money and feasibility
Whenever the committee dislikes the minister's answer and asks the official instead
Whenever the official is the most senior person in the department present
Whenever the committee chair asks the official to give a personal view

questions.prompt: Which topic would an official usually be careful about discussing?

options.text: The published results of a department's pilot scheme
The structure of the department
A statement the minister made earlier in public
The detail of the advice given to ministers

questions.hint: Advice to ministers is generally confidential.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of a briefing pack for an appearance?

options.text: To give the witness a script that must be read out in answer to each question
To keep controversial subjects hidden from the committee in a closed section
To prepare likely questions, check facts and know what has been published
To record the voting history of each committee member for reference

questions.hint: Preparation supports accurate and honest evidence.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour would breach the Code during an appearance?

options.text: Giving an answer that is technically true but leaves a false impression
Declining to speculate on a hypothetical question that the minister has not considered
Saying the department will answer a detailed question in writing afterwards
Referring a question about the choice of policy to the minister

questions.prompt: A committee asks for a document the department would prefer not to release. How should the official respond?

options.text: Send an edited version without saying it has been edited
Explain any concerns and escalate, not ignore or quietly withhold it
Delay a reply until the committee loses interest
Say it does not exist

questions.hint: Handling requests is a formal matter and must be honest.

items.title: L7: Accounting officers and the four tests
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; Accounting Officer System Statement
items.body: Managing Public Money is the Treasury's guide to handling public funds. It describes the role of the accounting officer: the person, normally the permanent secretary or the chief executive of an arm's length body, who is personally accountable to Parliament for how the organisation's resources are used. Accounting officers are expected to meet four standards. Regularity means that spending complies with the legal authority granted by Parliament and with Treasury rules. Propriety means that spending meets the standards of public conduct, including the requirement to be fair, honest and free from impropriety, in ways that go beyond strict legality. Value for money means achieving the best use of resources to meet the objective, not just the cheapest option. Feasibility means that the proposal can realistically be delivered, as set out in its plans and timescales. If a minister proposes a course of action which the accounting officer thinks fails one of these tests, the accounting officer must first set out their concerns in writing. If the minister wants to go ahead, the accounting officer can ask for a written instruction known as a ministerial direction. Once given, the accounting officer follows the direction, since the minister is accountable for the policy, but copies the direction to the Comptroller and Auditor General, who may report it to Parliament. Feasibility objections are the most common reason for directions. Ministerial directions are rare, which shows how seriously they are taken. Officials supporting the accounting officer should make sure advice on these tests is clear and recorded.

questions.prompt: A project would be legal and cheap but would pay public money to a firm run by a minister's relative with no competition. Which standard does it most clearly challenge?

options.text: Feasibility
Regularity
Value for money
Propriety

questions.hint: Propriety goes beyond legality to standards of conduct.

questions.prompt: Which test asks whether spending complies with Parliament's authorisation and Treasury rules?

options.text: Feasibility
Regularity
Value for money
Propriety

questions.hint: Regularity is compliance with legal authority.

questions.prompt: What is the first step if an accounting officer has doubts about a proposal the minister wants to pursue?

options.text: Set out the concerns in writing to the minister
Refuse to start any work related to the proposal until the minister withdraws it
Tell the Public Accounts Committee at once, before speaking to the minister
Tell the press, so that the public can hear the concerns before money is spent

questions.hint: Concerns are first put to the minister in writing.

questions.prompt: What does a ministerial direction require the accounting officer to do?

options.text: Resign from the post, since the minister has overridden their professional advice
Seek approval from the Civil Service Commission before carrying out the instruction
Carry out the minister's instruction and send a copy to the Comptroller and Auditor General
Publish the direction in the department's annual report and do nothing more

questions.hint: The accounting officer complies and the direction goes to the C&AG.

questions.prompt: Why are ministerial directions seen as an important safeguard?

options.text: They stop ministers from making any decisions that officials have criticised
They allow officials to overrule ministers whenever value for money is in doubt
They move responsibility for the policy to the Treasury once it is signed
They record who took responsibility when advice was set aside

questions.prompt: A scheme is projected to give the best value for the money but timescales are unrealistic. Which test is most at risk?

options.text: Regularity
Feasibility
Propriety
Value for money

questions.hint: Feasibility asks whether it can be delivered.

questions.prompt: Which statement about value for money is correct?

options.text: It means the cheapest option in all circumstances, whatever the quality
It means the highest quality option, whatever it costs
Value for money means the best overall use of resources to achieve the objective
It means the option the Treasury prefers

questions.hint: Value for money weighs costs and benefits.

questions.prompt: Who is normally the accounting officer for an executive agency?

options.text: Its chief executive
The minister
The chair of its board
The local MP

questions.hint: Chief executives account for their agencies.

items.title: L7: How a Bill becomes an Act
items.source: UK Parliament, How laws are made; GOV.UK, Guide to making legislation
items.body: Primary legislation is made by Parliament in the form of Acts. A government Bill usually begins as a policy decision by ministers, written up in instructions to Parliamentary Counsel, the specialist lawyers who draft Bills. Departments have Bill teams that coordinate the work with lawyers, policy officials and the Cabinet Office. Before it is introduced, a Bill needs clearance from the relevant Cabinet committee, so the whole government is content. In Parliament a Bill passes through a series of stages in each House: first reading, second reading, where the main principles are debated, committee stage, where detailed examination takes place, report stage, and third reading. After one House has passed it, it goes to the other House to go through the same process. If the Houses disagree on the wording, the Bill can go between them until they agree. Once both Houses are content, the King gives Royal Assent and it becomes an Act. Government departments publish explanatory notes and impact assessments with a Bill. Many Acts give ministers powers to make secondary legislation, usually in the form of statutory instruments, which fill in the detail. Secondary legislation is subject to parliamentary procedures but gets less debate than Bills. Officials must make sure the powers used are within the Act, since a minister who goes beyond the powers can be challenged in court by judicial review. After Royal Assent, an Act may come into force straight away, on a set date or when a minister makes a commencement order.

questions.prompt: Who drafts government Bills?

options.text: The Government Legal Department
The Speaker's office
Parliamentary Counsel
The Civil Service Commission

questions.hint: Parliamentary Counsel are the drafting specialists.

questions.prompt: Which stage of a Bill involves the main principles being debated?

options.text: First reading, when the Bill's title is read and the principles are debated
Second reading
Report stage, when the Bill's principles are first discussed by all members
Third reading, when the House decides whether the main principle is acceptable

questions.hint: Second reading is the debate on principles.

questions.prompt: A Bill passes through the Commons and is sent to the Lords. What happens next?

options.text: It becomes an Act straight away
It returns to the department for a new impact assessment
It goes to the Supreme Court for approval
It goes through a similar series of stages in the Lords

questions.prompt: What is secondary legislation?

options.text: Detailed rules made by ministers using powers given in an Act
A Bill that is introduced by a backbench MP rather than by the government
A second draft of a Bill after it has been amended in committee
Guidance for the public that is published on GOV.UK once an Act is in force

questions.prompt: What does Royal Assent do?

options.text: Turns the Bill into an Act
Starts the committee stage
Guarantees that the Act comes into force at once
Allows ministers to bypass Parliament

questions.prompt: A minister uses a power in a statutory instrument which goes beyond what the Act allows. What might follow?

options.text: The Speaker would withdraw it at once, because it exceeds the power in the Act
A court could quash it through judicial review
The Cabinet Secretary would amend it quietly so that it falls within the Act
Nothing would follow, because Parliament has already seen the instrument

questions.hint: Powers must stay within the Act.

questions.prompt: Why do departments publish explanatory notes and impact assessments with a Bill?

options.text: To avoid any need for debate, because the Bill is explained in advance
To satisfy the Speaker's office, which must approve every government Bill
To help Parliament and the public understand the Bill and its effects
To replace the need for Royal Assent once the notes have been published

questions.prompt: What is a commencement order for?

options.text: To ask Parliament to debate an Act again after Royal Assent has been given
To amend an Act after it has become law, without a new Bill
To give an Act Royal Assent in the name of the Crown
To bring an Act, or part of it, into force on a set date

questions.hint: Some Acts are brought into force by order.

items.title: L7: The policy cycle and appraisal
items.source: HM Treasury, The Green Book; The Magenta Book
items.body: Policy-making in government follows a broad cycle: identify a problem, understand the evidence, develop options, appraise them, decide, implement, and evaluate. The Green Book is the Treasury's guidance on appraising and evaluating policies, programmes and projects. It asks officials to set out the rationale for intervention, say what the objectives are, list a long list of options and narrow it to a short list, and compare costs and benefits. The Five Case Model is used for business cases and asks for the strategic case, the economic case, the commercial case, the financial case and the management case. Appraisal looks at the costs and benefits over time, often adjusting for the fact that benefits in the future are worth less than those now, using a discount rate. It also accounts for risks, optimism bias and the effect on different groups. The Magenta Book is the guidance on evaluation. It says evaluation should be planned at the start, with clear questions, so that evidence is collected while the policy runs. An evaluation can look at the process, the impact and the value for money. Officials should be open about evidence gaps and about the limits of the analysis. Departments often consult interested groups before deciding. Consultation should be clear, give enough time for responses, and the department should publish its response afterwards. Policy officials work with analysts, such as economists, statisticians, social researchers and operational researchers, who provide evidence and challenge assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which document provides Treasury guidance on appraising policies and projects?

options.text: The Magenta Book
The Orange Book
Managing Public Money
The Green Book

questions.hint: The Green Book covers appraisal; the Magenta Book covers evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the Five Case Model?

options.text: The political case
The commercial case
The legal case
The media case

questions.hint: The five cases are strategic, economic, commercial, financial and management.

questions.prompt: Why does appraisal often apply a discount rate?

options.text: Because benefits in the future are valued less than those received now
Because costs always fall over time as the project becomes established
Because the Treasury must receive a discount from suppliers on each contract
Because benefits are guaranteed only for the first year of a policy

questions.hint: Time preference is built into appraisal.

questions.prompt: When should evaluation be planned?

options.text: After the policy has ended, so that the full outcome is known
Only if a select committee asks the department to evaluate it
At the start, so evidence can be collected while the policy runs
Only if the policy appears to fail and the minister asks for review

questions.prompt: What does optimism bias mean in appraisal?

options.text: A preference shown by ministers for optimistic officials when they choose advisers
A bias in how consultation responses are counted when they are mostly favourable
The tendency to underestimate costs and time and overestimate benefits
A rule that makes the cheapest option look the best when appraised

questions.prompt: A consultation is sent out with only one week to respond and is not published afterwards. What is the main problem?

options.text: It is too short, but otherwise acceptable since the Act sets no minimum period
It breaks the Official Secrets Act because the document was unpublished
It is unlawful in all cases and the policy would have to be withdrawn
It does not give enough time or feedback, so it is not meaningful consultation

questions.hint: Good consultation allows time and publishes a response.

questions.prompt: What does an economic case in a business case set out?

options.text: The proposed contract terms and how the supplier will be chosen
The costs and benefits of the options for society as a whole
How the project will be managed and what governance it will have
The legal power on which the policy depends, and who will enforce it

questions.hint: The economic case is about value for money.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation type looks at whether a policy achieved its intended effect?

options.text: Impact evaluation
Process evaluation
Procurement evaluation
Consultation review

items.title: L7: Legal risk and judicial review
items.source: Government Legal Department; Judicial Review Handbook; Civil Service Code
items.body: Civil servants must comply with the law and uphold the administration of justice, as the Civil Service Code says. Government decisions can be challenged in court by judicial review, where a judge examines whether a public body acted lawfully. The court does not decide whether a decision was right on the merits, but whether it was made lawfully. The usual grounds are illegality, where the decision-maker misunderstood the law or acted beyond their powers; irrationality, where the decision was so unreasonable that no reasonable decision-maker could have made it; and procedural impropriety, where a fair process was not followed, for example by failing to consult when required or by being biased. Legitimate expectation and breach of human rights are also important arguments. When a decision may be risky, officials seek legal advice from departmental lawyers, who are often part of the Government Legal Department. Legal advice is generally privileged, which means it is protected from disclosure, and officials should treat it carefully and not circulate it widely. Good decision-making reduces risk: record reasons, consider relevant factors, ignore irrelevant ones, follow statutory procedure, consult where required, and give people a chance to respond before an adverse decision. Where a legal challenge is possible, there is a duty of candour, meaning the department must disclose relevant material to the court honestly, including documents that are unhelpful to its case. Officials involved should preserve documents and not delete or alter anything.

questions.prompt: Which ground of judicial review applies when a decision-maker misunderstands the law?

options.text: Irrationality
Procedural impropriety
Proportionality
Illegality

questions.hint: Illegality covers errors of law and acting beyond powers.

questions.prompt: What does a judicial review court primarily decide?

options.text: Whether the decision was the best one
Whether the decision was made lawfully
Whether the minister should resign
Whether Parliament should amend the law

questions.prompt: A decision is made without hearing from the person it affects, when the law required a chance to respond. Which ground fits best?

options.text: Procedural impropriety
Illegality
Irrationality
Legitimate expectation

questions.prompt: What does the duty of candour require?

options.text: The department to settle every claim made against it to avoid a hearing
Officials to publish their legal advice so that the public can judge it
The department to disclose relevant material honestly, including unhelpful documents
Ministers to explain the reasoning behind the decision to Parliament

questions.prompt: Why should officials not circulate legal advice widely?

options.text: Because all legal advice is secret under the Official Secrets Act 1989
Legal advice is privileged and sharing it can risk losing that protection
Because lawyers must approve every email that mentions their advice
Because legal advice belongs to the Treasury, not the department

questions.prompt: A legal challenge to a decision is expected. What should the team do with its documents?

options.text: Preserve them and not delete or alter anything
Remove drafts to reduce confusion
Move documents to personal storage for safety
Destroy emails more than a week old

questions.prompt: Which action reduces the risk of a successful challenge?

options.text: Making the decision quickly so that there is little time for challenge
Relying on informal discussions, which are harder to scrutinise
Recording reasons and considering relevant factors
Leaving out the comments of an applicant, to keep the file simple

questions.prompt: A decision is so unreasonable that no sensible decision-maker could reach it. Which ground applies?

options.text: Illegality
Procedural impropriety
Candour
Irrationality

items.title: L7: Public appointments and boards
items.source: Governance Code on Public Appointments; Commissioner for Public Appointments
items.body: Many arm's length bodies are led by boards whose chairs and members are public appointees. Most senior appointments are made by ministers, but the process must follow the Governance Code on Public Appointments. The Code's principles include ministerial responsibility, selection on merit, openness, diversity, assessment of candidates against published criteria, and fairness. The Commissioner for Public Appointments is independent of government and regulates the process, can review and audit appointments, and reports on compliance. For the most senior roles, such as the chairs of major bodies, a pre-appointment hearing by a select committee may take place. The committee gives its views, though the final decision lies with the minister. Advertising the post publicly, an advisory assessment panel that includes an independent member and a shortlist with scored interviews are usual features. The panel recommends appointable candidates, and the minister chooses among them. Ministers can decide not to appoint anyone and ask for a new campaign. Appointees are expected to follow the Seven Principles of Public Life, known as the Nolan Principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership. They must declare interests, and conflicts are managed by the board. Board members are not civil servants and are accountable for the body's governance, while the chief executive is responsible for running it and for accountability as the accounting officer. Ministers do not run these appointments on political lines, and political activity of candidates must be declared openly but is not by itself a bar.

questions.prompt: What does the Commissioner for Public Appointments do?

options.text: Regulates and audits the public appointments process
Appoints the chairs of all arm's length bodies on behalf of ministers
Sets the pay of board members across all public bodies
Chairs the select committees that hold pre-appointment hearings

questions.hint: The Commissioner is the independent regulator.

questions.prompt: A minister is given a list of appointable candidates by an assessment panel. What may the minister do?

options.text: Appoint anyone, including someone not shortlisted
Allow the panel to make the final choice
Choose among them or ask for a new campaign
Appoint the candidate with the longest CV

questions.prompt: What is a pre-appointment hearing?

options.text: A meeting of the board held before an appointment is made, to agree the shortlist
A court hearing in which a judge checks that an appointment was lawful
A panel interview in which candidates present to the assessment panel
A select committee hearing where it gives its view on a preferred candidate

questions.hint: The committee gives views but the minister decides.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the Nolan Principles?

options.text: Loyalty to the party
Selflessness
Efficiency
Neutrality

questions.hint: Selflessness is the first of the seven.

questions.prompt: A candidate for a board role has political links. What does the Code require?

options.text: The activity is declared openly but is not by itself a bar to appointment
The candidate must not be considered, because political links are a bar
The candidate must resign from the party before they can be interviewed
The candidate must be given priority so the board is politically balanced

questions.prompt: Which statement about board members is correct?

options.text: They are civil servants in the sponsor department and take its instructions
They are accountable only to the chief executive of the body
They run the body day to day, as executives do
They are not civil servants and are accountable for governance

questions.prompt: Which feature typically supports merit in an appointment?

options.text: A conversation between the minister and one friend
Selection by seniority
Assessment against published criteria with scored interviews
Choosing from a list prepared by lobbyists

questions.prompt: A board member discovers a conflict with a contract the board is discussing. What should happen?

options.text: They stay quiet if the contract is fairly priced and the board benefits
They declare it and the board manages it, for instance by excluding them from the item
They resign immediately from the board, whatever the circumstances
They report it only to the press office, which tells the board

items.title: L7: Who counts as a civil servant?
items.source: Civil Service Commission; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010; GOV.UK, Civil Service statistics
items.body: Not everyone who works for the public sector is a civil servant. Civil servants are Crown servants who work for the government and the departments it controls. The Civil Service comprises the Home Civil Service, the Diplomatic Service and the Northern Ireland Civil Service, along with a few other groups. The Home Civil Service includes staff in UK government departments and agencies and staff of the Scottish and Welsh Governments. Many other public employees are not civil servants: NHS staff are employed by NHS bodies, teachers by schools and local authorities, police officers hold the office of constable, members of the armed forces serve under the Crown in separate arrangements, and local council staff work for local government. Employees of non-departmental public bodies often work under their own terms and conditions. The distinction matters because the Civil Service Code applies to civil servants, while others have their own codes, such as police standards or the Nolan Principles for public life. A civil servant's terms are set by the department under the Civil Service Management Code, rather than by Parliament. This matters when a member of the public asks who is responsible. A caller who says that a local housing officer was rude should be told that the council handles the complaint, since the council, not a central department, employs the officer. Likewise, an issue with a hospital goes to the NHS trust. Civil servants must be clear about which organisation is responsible. They must not pretend to speak for a body that is not theirs.

questions.prompt: Which group is not made up of civil servants?

options.text: Staff in the Home Office
Staff of the Scottish Government
Staff of the Foreign Office posted overseas
Local council housing officers

questions.prompt: A caller complains about a nurse at their local hospital. Where should it normally go?

options.text: The Cabinet Office
The Civil Service Commission
The NHS body running the hospital
The Treasury

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Northern Ireland Civil Service is correct?

options.text: It is part of the Home Civil Service and shares its Code and management
It is separate from the Home Civil Service
It is run by the Scottish Government on behalf of the Northern Ireland Executive
It has no civil servants of its own, as work is done by the Home Office

questions.hint: NICS is a separate civil service.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter whether someone is a civil servant?

options.text: The Civil Service Code applies to civil servants, while others have their own codes
Only civil servants pay income tax on their earnings from public work
Only civil servants may vote in elections, because of their public role
Only civil servants are allowed to work for the public in government

questions.prompt: Who sets civil servants' terms and conditions?

options.text: Departments under the Civil Service Management Code
Parliament, which approves the terms for each grade in an annual Act
The courts, which settle terms when disputes arise between departments
The Prime Minister personally, by writing to each department each year

questions.hint: Terms are set under the Management Code.

questions.prompt: A member of the public complains about a council planning decision. What should you tell them?

options.text: The department will overturn it, because planning is a national function
The Prime Minister's office handles complaints about planning decisions
The council is responsible, and you can explain how to complain to it
The Civil Service Commission investigates councils' planning decisions

questions.hint: Be clear which organisation is responsible.

questions.prompt: Which group serve in separate arrangements, not as civil servants?

options.text: Staff in the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
Staff in HMRC
Staff in the Welsh Government
The armed forces

questions.hint: The armed forces serve under their own arrangements.

questions.prompt: An official is asked about a decision by an independent regulator that is not their department. How should they respond?

options.text: Offer an opinion on the regulator's decision, to be as helpful as possible
Say it is for the regulator and, if possible, point to published information
Promise that the department will ask the regulator to change its decision
Say the department will take over the case because the caller is unhappy

questions.hint: Do not speak for another body.

items.title: L7: Sharing data between departments
items.source: UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018; ICO Data sharing code of practice
items.body: Government departments often hold data that other departments could use, for example to check eligibility for support. Sharing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Before data is shared, officials need a legal basis for processing personal data under the UK GDPR, such as performing a public task with a clear basis in law. Many sharing arrangements rely on legal gateways, which are provisions in legislation that permit or require sharing for defined purposes. Sharing must be limited to what is necessary and proportionate for that purpose, following the principle of data minimisation. Officials usually record the arrangement in a data sharing agreement, which sets out the purpose, what data is shared, how it is secured, how long it is kept and who is responsible. For new or high-risk sharing, a data protection impact assessment is carried out to identify and reduce risks to individuals. Departments must be open about what they do through privacy notices. People have rights, such as seeing their data, having inaccurate data corrected and, in some cases, objecting. Data security is vital: information must be shared through secure channels, classified correctly, and only with those who need it. If a breach happens, such as sending data to the wrong person, it must be reported to the data protection officer straight away because serious breaches must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours. Data should not be shared simply because a colleague asks informally or because it would be convenient. Passing data to a third party without a lawful basis is a breach of the law and the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: A colleague in another department emails to ask for a list of customers' addresses because it would be convenient for their project. What is the correct response?

options.text: Check there is a lawful basis and an agreement before sharing anything
Send it, since both departments are part of the same government
Send it but mark it Official so that it is handled correctly
Send half the list, to reduce the risk if it is misused

questions.hint: Sharing needs a lawful basis, not convenience.

questions.prompt: What does data minimisation require?

options.text: Sharing as much data as possible, so that nothing relevant is missed
Sharing only what is necessary and proportionate for the purpose
Deleting the data from the sending department once it has been shared
Sharing data only by post, which is thought to be safer

questions.hint: Only necessary data should be shared.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a legal gateway for data sharing?

options.text: A security door into a government building that restricts entry to staff
A form used by customers to make a subject access request
A list of approved suppliers who may receive government data
A provision in legislation that permits or requires data sharing for defined purposes

questions.prompt: When is a data protection impact assessment especially needed?

options.text: Only for routine email, which is the most common way data is shared
Only when a complaint has been made by someone about the sharing
For new or high-risk sharing, to identify and reduce risks to individuals
Only for data that is more than ten years old and about to be deleted

questions.prompt: You send a spreadsheet of claimants' details to the wrong recipient by mistake. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to see if the recipient replies before telling anyone about it
Report it immediately to the data protection officer or your manager
Ask the recipient to delete it and say nothing more to avoid fuss
Tell the affected claimants first, before involving the data protection officer

questions.prompt: By when must serious breaches be reported to the ICO?

options.text: Within 72 hours of becoming aware
Within 28 days, to allow for a full investigation
Within one year, at the end of the financial year
Within one working day, whatever the severity

questions.prompt: What does a data sharing agreement usually include?

options.text: The names of all customers whose data is shared, to be kept on file
Only the contact details of the people who signed the agreement
A list of the ministers who approved the sharing of data
The purpose, data shared, security, retention and who is responsible

questions.prompt: What is a privacy notice for?

options.text: To list the staff who can be phoned about data requests
To record a subject access request when it has been received
To tell people how their data is used
To authorise the sharing of data between two departments

items.title: L7: Delivery through contractors and partners
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money; Procurement Act 2023; Government Functional Standard on commercial
items.body: Departments often deliver services through private companies, charities and other partners. Even when a service is delivered by a contractor, the department remains accountable to Parliament and the public for the outcome. Procurement is governed by public procurement law, which requires fair, transparent competition, equal treatment and value for money. The Procurement Act 2023 reformed the rules for most public contracts. Procurement officers must follow the rules and keep records of decisions. A contract sets out what the supplier must deliver, how performance is measured, what happens if standards are not met, and how the contract can end. Contract managers monitor delivery using key performance indicators, meet suppliers regularly and manage risks. They also check that the supplier meets obligations on data protection, security and treating customers fairly. If a contractor makes an error that harms a customer, the customer's complaint goes to the department, and officials cannot simply say that it is the supplier's problem. A department should know how the supplier is performing, so that it can put things right and explain to ministers. Contract changes must follow the rules, as large changes may require a new competition. Direct awards without competition are allowed only in limited circumstances, such as genuine urgency, and must be justified and recorded. Officials who have been involved in a procurement must be careful about gifts and hospitality from bidders and suppliers. Cooling-off rules also limit how quickly staff can move to work for suppliers.

questions.prompt: A contractor delivering a department's helpline gives a customer wrong advice. Who is accountable to the public and Parliament?

options.text: The contractor alone, since it gave the advice under its contract
The customer, who ought to have checked the advice
The Treasury, which sets the rules for contracted services
The department, which remains accountable for the service

questions.prompt: What is a key performance indicator used for?

options.text: To rank bidders in a tender according to price and quality
To measure how well a supplier is delivering against the contract
To set the price of a contract before the tender is run
To record complaints made by staff about the contract

questions.prompt: A department wishes to award a new contract directly without competition. When is this normally allowed?

options.text: In limited circumstances, such as genuine urgency, with justification recorded
Whenever the supplier has done good work for the department in the past
Whenever the minister prefers a particular supplier
Whenever the value is under a million pounds

questions.prompt: Why must contract changes follow the rules?

options.text: Because every change must go to the Treasury
Because the supplier must approve each change
A large change may need a new competition
Because changes can only be made annually

questions.hint: Large changes can undermine fair competition.

questions.prompt: Which factor must procurement law require?

options.text: Fair and transparent competition and equal treatment
A preference for local firms so that spending benefits the area
The lowest price in every case, whatever the quality
A preference for the existing supplier unless it performs badly

questions.hint: Fair competition and value for money.

questions.prompt: A bidder invites the procurement lead to a hospitality event during a live tender. What should the official do?

options.text: Accept if the event is open to the public
Accept and declare it afterwards
Accept but pay for their own lunch
Decline and record the offer

questions.hint: Hospitality from bidders in a live tender risks the appearance of bias.

questions.prompt: Which statement about complaints is correct?

options.text: Customers must complain to the supplier only, because it provides the service
Customers complain to the department, which must resolve the issue even if the supplier is at fault
The Treasury deals with all complaints about contractors
The courts must decide all complaints about contracted services

questions.prompt: What do cooling-off rules do?

options.text: Restrict suppliers' pricing in the period after a contract is awarded
Delay payments to suppliers while quality is checked
Limit how soon staff can move to work for a supplier
Stop staff attending meetings with suppliers after the contract starts

questions.hint: They manage conflicts and perceived influence.

items.title: L7: Complaints that reach the Ombudsman
items.source: Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman; Parliamentary Commissioner Act 1967
items.body: A department's complaints process usually has stages: an initial response from the team involved, a review by someone more senior, and sometimes a final stage handled by an independent complaint examiner or a director. If the person is still unhappy once the department's process is complete, they can ask the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman, known as PHSO, to investigate. The Ombudsman is independent of government and investigates complaints that a UK government department or other listed public body has treated someone unfairly or provided a poor service, causing injustice. The Ombudsman does not decide whether policy is right or wrong, and cannot normally investigate matters that are already before a court or tribunal, or where there is a right of appeal to a tribunal that it would be reasonable to use. The Ombudsman can recommend that the body apologise, put things right and change processes, and can recommend financial redress. Departments are not legally bound to follow the recommendations but almost always accept them, and the Ombudsman can report to Parliament if they do not. The Ombudsman looks at maladministration, which includes delay, failure to follow procedures, giving misleading advice, and failure to put things right. Officials should respond to the Ombudsman's enquiries promptly and honestly, provide full records and learn from the findings. A good first-stage reply is clear, apologises where there is a fault, explains what will be done, and tells the person about the next stage. A department that learns from complaints can improve services.

questions.prompt: When can a person usually take a complaint to the Ombudsman?

options.text: After the department's own complaints process has been completed
Immediately, without trying the department's own process first
Only after a court has ruled on the complaint
Only through the Prime Minister's office, which refers cases onwards

questions.hint: Departments get the first chance to put things right.

questions.prompt: Which of these is something the Ombudsman does not normally decide?

options.text: Whether a department gave misleading advice
Whether a government policy is right or wrong
Whether a department was unreasonably slow
Whether a department failed to follow its own procedures

questions.hint: The Ombudsman looks at maladministration, not policy merits.

questions.prompt: The Ombudsman upholds a complaint and recommends an apology and a payment. What is the department's position?

options.text: It is legally bound to follow it and must do so within 28 days
It can ignore it, with no further consequence for the department
It must first seek court approval before following it
It is not legally bound to follow it but almost always does

questions.hint: Recommendations are not legally binding but are normally accepted.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of maladministration?

options.text: Making a policy the complainant dislikes
Rejecting an appeal in line with the rules
Failing to put right a known error
Using a standard letter

questions.hint: Failing to put things right is classic maladministration.

questions.prompt: What makes a good first-stage complaint reply?

options.text: Short and defensive, so that nothing is said which could be used against the department
Clear, apologises where there was a fault, explains actions and next stage
Silent on the fault so as not to admit liability
Brief, referring the person to their MP for any further action

questions.hint: Good replies are clear and honest.

questions.prompt: Why would the Ombudsman usually decline a case that is before a court?

options.text: Because courts and the Ombudsman cannot work together
Because the Ombudsman cannot cover courts
Because the court is the proper place to decide it
Because the Ombudsman takes only financial complaints

questions.prompt: What should an official do when the Ombudsman asks for records?

options.text: Provide a summary only
Delay while the department prepares its defence
Ask the complainant for consent
Respond promptly with full and accurate records

questions.prompt: What benefit comes from analysing complaints?

options.text: Departments can see patterns and improve services
Departments can identify which staff to blame for mistakes
Complaints would no longer be needed from the public
Ministers could avoid scrutiny from Parliament over service failures

items.title: L7: Recruitment exceptions and fairness
items.body: The Civil Service Commission publishes the Recruitment Principles, which require that appointments are made on merit after fair and open competition. Merit means choosing the person who best meets the criteria for the job. Fair means that candidates are assessed on the same basis and without bias. Open means that jobs are advertised so that anyone eligible can apply. The Principles allow some exceptions to open competition, which are set out in the Principles and must be properly recorded and sometimes reported to the Commission. Examples include short-term appointments, some secondments, and schemes designed to help people who are under-represented or face barriers, such as particular schemes for disabled people. Exceptions must still meet the merit principle. A department may also use internal advertising for some posts, but it must follow its own rules and make sure no one is treated unfairly. Panel members must be trained and assess candidates against the published criteria using evidence from the Success Profiles, which combine behaviours, strengths, ability, experience and technical skills. The Commission audits departments' recruitment and can investigate complaints from candidates who think there was a breach. Candidates may complain first to the department and then to the Commission. The Principles require that records are kept to show how decisions were made. Reasonable adjustments must be offered to disabled candidates, and the process must not discriminate. Where a department wants to offer a job to someone on the basis of who they know, it breaks the Principles. The Commission can also require changes to practice where it finds problems.

questions.prompt: What does 'open' mean in the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Panel meetings are open to the public who wish to observe
All applications are published online after the closing date
Jobs are advertised so that anyone eligible can apply
Interviews are recorded and may be shared with the candidates

questions.prompt: A manager wants to hire a former colleague into a permanent post without advertising. What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem, because managers can appoint anyone with the skills
It would normally breach fair and open competition unless an exception applies and is recorded
There is no problem if the former colleague is highly qualified for the job
It would be fine if the post is at a junior grade

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of an exception?

options.text: A permanent post given to a friend
A promotion given to the longest-serving team member
A job offered by the minister's office
A short-term appointment

questions.prompt: What do the Success Profiles combine?

options.text: Behaviours, strengths, ability, experience and technical skills
Salary, grade, location, hours and benefits
Qualifications, age, gender, interest and hobbies
Loyalty, speed, friendliness, leadership and seniority

questions.hint: The five elements are the Success Profiles.

questions.prompt: A candidate believes the process was unfair. What are the usual steps?

options.text: Complain to the department first and then, if unresolved, to the Commission
Go straight to the press, to put pressure on the department
Complain to the Treasury, which oversees the department's staffing
Ask the minister to reverse the decision after the process has ended

questions.prompt: What must departments do for a disabled candidate who asks for a change to the process?

options.text: Refuse, in order to keep the process uniform
Offer a different job instead
Consider and make reasonable adjustments
Ask for medical evidence of every need

questions.prompt: Why are records of recruitment decisions kept?

options.text: To pass candidates' details to other departments
To show how decisions were made and allow audit and challenge
To fix the start date
To record the panel's salary

questions.prompt: What can the Commission do if it finds problems in a department's recruitment?

options.text: Cancel the appointment of a minister who has breached the Principles
Reduce the department's budget until recruitment improves
Remove the permanent secretary from post
Audit, investigate and require changes to practice

items.title: L7: Announcements and Parliament
items.source: Ministerial Code; Cabinet Manual; House of Commons Speaker's statements
items.body: The Ministerial Code says that when Parliament is sitting, the most important announcements of government policy should be made in the first instance to Parliament. This shows respect for Parliament and gives MPs the chance to question ministers. It is why officials preparing a major policy announcement must think carefully about timing and sequencing. Ministers commonly use a written ministerial statement for announcements that do not need an oral statement, or an oral statement, which is followed by questions from MPs. Material is typically released at the same time as the statement is made, and not before, which includes press releases, GOV.UK updates and social media. Officials often prepare an announcement plan setting out the order of events, who needs advance notice, for example the devolved governments if the matter affects them, and what documents will be published. They also take care over market-sensitive information, such as economic data or tax changes, which must not be released early because it could affect financial markets or give someone an unfair advantage. Budget measures are especially sensitive. Deliberate or careless leaks of announcements can lead to criticism from the Speaker, who can demand that a minister explain. Officials must therefore protect advance copies, restrict access to those who need it, and use agreed embargo times for press. If a story appears early, officials should inform the private office and the press office, who will decide what to do. The Speaker may also criticise ministers for announcing a policy to the media before telling MPs.

questions.prompt: A minister plans to announce a major policy change while Parliament is sitting. Where should the announcement normally be made first?

options.text: In a newspaper interview
On social media
In Parliament
At a press conference

questions.hint: The Ministerial Code puts Parliament first.

questions.prompt: What is an embargo time on a press release?

options.text: An agreed time before which a press release must not be published
A time limit on parliamentary questions that applies to each department
A deadline by which appeals must be lodged against a decision
The end of the pre-election period, when normal business resumes

questions.prompt: Why is market-sensitive information handled with special care?

options.text: Because the Speaker prefers it to be released only on certain days
Because it is always classified Top Secret under the security system
Because it is owned by the Treasury and cannot be used elsewhere
Early release could affect financial markets or give an unfair advantage

questions.hint: Market-sensitive material must not be released early.

questions.prompt: A story based on an unpublished announcement appears early in the press. What should an official do?

options.text: Confirm the story to the journalist, so it is accurate
Tell the private office and press office promptly
Delete the announcement plan so nothing else is leaked
Ask the newspaper to remove the story and stay quiet otherwise

questions.hint: Escalate so that the department can decide how to respond.

questions.prompt: Why do announcement plans often include notice to the devolved governments?

options.text: Because they must approve the announcement before it is made
Because the matter may affect devolved areas and they should hear before the public
Because they run Parliament and need to arrange time for the statement
Because the Speaker requires it before any statement can be given

questions.prompt: A minister gives details to the media before telling MPs. What might follow?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission will investigate the minister's conduct
The announcement becomes legally invalid and must be repeated
The department's budget is cut as a penalty
The Speaker may criticise the minister and require an explanation

questions.prompt: Which of these is released at the same time as a statement?

options.text: Press releases and GOV.UK updates
Documents marked Secret that explain the policy's background
Advice given to ministers in private before the announcement
The minister's diary for the day of the statement

questions.hint: Material is aligned to the announcement.

questions.prompt: How should advance copies of an announcement be handled?

options.text: Shared with all staff to prepare
Sent to colleagues by personal email
Restricted to those who need them and protected
Left on shared drives with open access

items.title: L7: Working across departments
items.source: Cabinet Office, Cabinet Manual; Civil Service guidance on cross-government working
items.body: Many problems cut across departmental boundaries: youth crime involves education, health, justice and local government; net zero involves energy, transport, business and housing. Government handles this through cross-departmental working. The Cabinet and its committees are the main forum for decisions that affect more than one department, based on the principle of collective responsibility, which means that decisions reached collectively are binding on all ministers. Officials support this through the Cabinet Office, which coordinates policy, and through cross-government groups and units. A lead department is normally named, which means one minister and department hold responsibility for coordinating delivery, even if other departments contribute. Departments agree roles in writing, share evidence, and resolve disagreements by escalating through the Director General to the permanent secretary and then to ministers if needed. The Treasury scrutinises spending decisions and must agree to any new spending, so officials engage it early. Before a department announces a policy that affects others, it seeks their agreement through a process known as clearance or write-round, where papers are circulated to relevant departments and comments are collected. Officials should be open about the limits of their department's views and avoid surprising colleagues in other departments. Joint working involves cultural differences, different systems and data, and different accountability, so clear governance matters. When a cross-government programme fails, accountability is a difficulty, so good programmes set out who is responsible for what.

questions.prompt: What does collective responsibility mean?

options.text: Decisions reached collectively are binding on all ministers
Every minister answers to Parliament for every department's decisions
Civil servants vote on decisions taken in the Cabinet
Ministers may publicly disagree with a decision once it is taken

questions.hint: It supports unity once a decision is made.

questions.prompt: What is a lead department?

options.text: The department with the largest budget in a joint programme
The department that employs the Prime Minister's private office
The department with overall responsibility for coordinating delivery
The department that audits the work of the others

questions.prompt: Your department wants to announce a policy which affects another department's responsibilities. What should happen first?

options.text: Announce it and let them respond
Seek the other department's agreement through clearance or write-round
Ask the press office to inform them after
Ask the Treasury to approve it for them

questions.prompt: Why should the Treasury be involved early?

options.text: Because it writes the Cabinet agenda
Because it drafts all legislation
Because it controls the media
New spending needs its agreement

questions.prompt: Two departments disagree on how to deliver a joint programme. What is the usual route to resolve it?

options.text: Escalate through senior officials, then ministers if needed
Ask the Speaker to decide
Let the larger department decide
Pause the programme until an election

questions.hint: Disputes are escalated up the chain.

questions.prompt: What helps a cross-government programme to maintain accountability?

options.text: Giving every department equal responsibility for everything
Setting out who is responsible for what
Leaving responsibilities vague
Avoiding written agreements

questions.prompt: What is the Cabinet Office's main role in cross-government work?

options.text: Running all departments
Auditing departmental accounts
Appointing ministers
Coordinating policy and supporting the Cabinet

questions.prompt: An official in one department knows of a risk to another department's plan. What is best?

options.text: Wait until they ask
Tell the press
Tell colleagues in that department early rather than leave them surprised
Keep it private to protect their own department
